Definition: zero-volume windows are excluded by 0<|W_n|. The compact enlargement K={0} is allowed and gives zero boundary excess identically, satisfying its required ratio.

Definition: d=1 is included with positive-length Borel windows and compact subsets of R. One fixed window alone cannot meet the sequence condition |W_n| tending to infinity, but each individual W_n is required to have positive finite length.

Definition: zero-volume windows and bounded-volume sequences are excluded by strict positive finite volumes and divergence to infinity. A compact K consisting of only {0} is allowed and has identically zero boundary excess.

Definition: spatial sets are arbitrary bounded Borel windows, so there is no distinguished interval endpoint. Their boundary is nevertheless addressed by the required measurable excess (W_n+K) minus W_n and its ratio for every compact K, including singleton shifts.

Definition: AC_omega is explicitly assumed to obtain Lebesgue measurability of Borel windows. Positive volume ensures each window is nonempty; no points are selected from the family W_n or compact enlargements K.
Definition: calling (W_n) a Van Hove sequence entails positive finite volumes, volume divergence, measurable boundary excesses, and their zero relative limit for every compact K.
Definition: a bounded Borel sequence satisfying all the displayed positive-volume, divergence and compact-enlargement conditions is, by the given definition, a Van Hove sequence.
Definition: each W_n inherits strictly positive volume from the Van Hove sequence, so an empty averaging window is inadmissible and division by its volume is not performed.
Definition: X identically zero has absolutely integrable paths and yields bar X_Wn=0 on every positive-volume window; the exceptional-event convention also fixes zero.

Definition: a one-dimensional Van Hove sequence in R is permitted and the normalization is by its length. A single observation is not required because the field average is a spatial integral, not a sample average over observations.

Definition: a deterministic constant field a gives bar X_Wn=a on every positive-volume window, and has no path-integrability exceptional event. Zero-volume normalization remains excluded by the inherited Van Hove definition.

Definition: integration is over the entire specified Borel W_n, with its actual boundary convention; no interval or frequency endpoint is specified. Boundaries of positive measure are included exactly according to membership in W_n, and positive volume protects normalization.

Definition: the inherited AC_omega supplies the Lebesgue measure interface for the Borel windows. The average is a section integral and has a fixed zero extension on the exceptional null event; no choice of a representative point from a window is made.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and assume the Axiom of Countable Choice
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). By
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]], every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^d$
is Lebesgue measurable under this assumption; by
[[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], $|\cdot|$ is the resulting
complete Lebesgue measure. A **Van Hove sequence of spatial windows** is a
sequence $(W_n)_{n\ge1}$ of bounded Borel sets
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) in $\mathbb R^d$ with
$0<|W_n|<\infty$ for every $n$, $|W_n|\to\infty$, and
$$\frac{|(W_n+K)\setminus W_n|}{|W_n|}\longrightarrow0 \quad\text{for every compact }K\subseteq\mathbb R^d.$$
Here $|E|$ is Lebesgue measure when $E$ is Lebesgue measurable, and
$W_n+K:=\{x+y:x\in W_n,\ y\in K\}$. As part of the condition, each boundary
excess $(W_n+K)\setminus W_n$ in the display is required to be Lebesgue
measurable. Thus the window volume diverges while every fixed compact spatial
enlargement adds a negligible relative volume.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $(W_n)$ be a Van Hove sequence in $\mathbb R^d$ as in
[[def-van-hove-window-sequence]], under its $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ assumption.
The Borel-measurability result makes each $W_n$ Lebesgue measurable, and the
complete-measure result supplies the Lebesgue measure used below. On a
probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]), let
$(X(s))_{s\in\mathbb R^d}$ be a real random field in the coordinatewise
sense of [[def-random-field-stationarity-covariance-and-variogram]]; its
coordinates are real random variables
([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]) such that the map
$(s,\omega)\mapsto X(s,\omega)$ is measurable for
$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)\otimes\mathcal F$
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). For $W_n$, assume that
$\int_{W_n}|X(s,\omega)|\,ds<\infty$ for almost every $\omega$. Define the
**spatial window average** on that full-measure event by
$$\bar X_{W_n}(\omega):=\frac1{|W_n|}\int_{W_n}X(s,\omega)\,ds,$$
and set it to $0$ on the measurable exceptional null set. Here $|W_n|$ and
the integral use $d$-dimensional Lebesgue measure, and a sample path means the
function $s\mapsto X(s,\omega)$. The theorem
[[thm-van-hove-window-average-l2-consistency]] establishes this integrability
and measurability from its stated second-moment hypotheses.

Let $T\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, have its relative Borel sigma-algebra, and
let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be one probability space. A **real random
field** indexed by $T$ is a family $X=(X(s))_{s\in T}$ of real random variables
$X(s):\Omega\to\mathbb R$ on that space. This is coordinate measurability:
each map $(s,\omega)\mapsto X(s,\omega)$ with $s$ fixed is measurable in
$\omega$. The field is **jointly measurable** when the map
$(s,\omega)\mapsto X(s,\omega)$ from
$(T\times\Omega,\mathcal B(T)\otimes\mathcal F)$ to
$(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ is measurable. Joint measurability is an
additional hypothesis when a spatial Lebesgue integral is used; it is not part
of coordinate measurability.

Write $\mathcal L(X(s_1),\ldots,X(s_n))$ for the pushforward law of a finite
coordinate tuple ([[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]],
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). The field is **strictly stationary** on $T$ when, for every
finite tuple $s_1,\ldots,s_n\in T$ and every $u\in\mathbb R^d$ for which
$s_i+u\in T$ for all $i$, these joint laws are invariant under the common
translation $s_i\mapsto s_i+u$. This extends the integer-shift convention for
time series in [[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]] to spatial
indices.

Write $T-T:=\{t-s:s,t\in T\}$ for the set of displacements realized by pairs
of sites.

The field is **wide stationary** when every $X(s)$ is square-integrable, its
mean is one constant $m$, and there is a function $C:T-T\to\mathbb R$ such
that
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X(s),X(t))=C(t-s)\qquad(s,t\in T).$$
For a wide-stationary field on all of $\mathbb R^d$, it is **wide isotropic**
when $C(h)$ depends only on the Euclidean norm $\|h\|$.

For $h\in T-T$ and any $s$ with $s,s+h\in T$, put
$\Delta_hX(s):=X(s+h)-X(s)$. The field is **intrinsically stationary of order
two** when for each $h\in T-T$ the first and second raw moments of
$\Delta_hX(s)$ are finite and independent of the admissible starting site
$s$. Here these moments are $\mathbb E[\Delta_hX(s)]$ and
$\mathbb E[(\Delta_hX(s))^2]$. The common second moment defines the
**variogram**
$$\gamma(h):=\frac12\mathbb E[(\Delta_hX(s))^2].$$
The mean increment may depend on $h$ and need not be zero; no finite second
moment of the field levels themselves is required by this definition.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

The two displayed integrals are well-defined by
[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $1\le p\le\infty$. For real random variables whose classes lie in
$L^p(\mathbb P)$ as defined by [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]],
write $X_n\to X$ **in $L^p$** when
$$\|[X_n]-[X]\|_{L^p(\mathbb P)}\longrightarrow0.$$ 
For $p<\infty$, this norm is
$$\|[X_n]-[X]\|_{L^p(\mathbb P)}=\bigl(\mathbb E|X_n-X|^p\bigr)^{1/p};$$
for $p=\infty$, it is the essential-supremum norm. Thus the assertion concerns
almost-everywhere equivalence classes, not chosen representatives.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces, and let
$$f : X \times Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$$
be $(\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B,\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R}))$-measurable.
Then $f_x : Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal B$-measurable for every
$x \in X$, and $f^y : X \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable
for every $y \in Y$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

derivations.claim: By [F11], Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^d$ is sigma-finite under the assumed $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Its restriction to $W_n$ is finite by [A1], and the probability measure has total mass $1$. Thus all measure factors used below satisfy the sigma-finiteness hypotheses of [F5] and [F6], including the unbounded lag-space factor in $W_n\times\mathbb R^d$. For every $s$, [F4] with $V=1$ gives $\mathbb E|X(s)|\le(\mathbb E[X(s)^2])^{1/2}=M<\infty$, where $M$ is constant by the stated first- and second-order stationarity. The map $(s,\omega)\mapsto |X(s,\omega)|$ is product-measurable; Tonelli [F5] gives $\mathbb E\int_{W_n}|X(s)|\,ds =\int_{W_n}\mathbb E|X(s)|\,ds\le M|W_n|<\infty.$ Therefore the sample path is absolutely integrable almost surely. Tonelli also makes the event where this integral is finite measurable; its probability is one. Applying Tonelli separately to $X^+$ and $X^-$ makes both section integrals measurable, and their difference on that event, extended by zero on its null complement as in [A2], is measurable.

Since $\int_{W_n}\mathbb E|X(s)|\,ds<\infty$, Fubini [F6] applies to $X$ on $W_n\times\Omega$. Its constant mean gives $\mathbb E[\bar X_{W_n}]=\frac1{|W_n|}\int_{W_n}\mathbb E[X(s)]\,ds =\frac1{|W_n|}\int_{W_n}\mu\,ds=\mu.$

Put $Z(s):=X(s)-\mu$. The rectangle-preimage argument in [F9] makes $(s,t,\omega)\mapsto Z(s,\omega)Z(t,\omega)$ product-measurable. By [F4], $\mathbb E|Z(s)Z(t)|\le C(0)$ for all $s,t$. Iterated Tonelli [F5] therefore gives a finite integral, at most $C(0)|W_n|^2$, of the absolute pair product over $W_n\times W_n\times\Omega$. Each $\Omega$-section is integrable by this bound, so Fubini [F6] makes $(s,t)\mapsto\mathbb E[Z(s)Z(t)]$ measurable; it equals $C(t-s)$ by [F2]. A second Fubini calculation yields $\mathbb E\bigl[(\bar X_{W_n}-\mu)^2\bigr] =\frac1{|W_n|^2}\int_{W_n}\int_{W_n}C(t-s)\,dt\,ds.$ This also proves $\bar X_{W_n}\in L^2$.

Define $q_n(h):=|W_n\cap(W_n-h)|/|W_n|$. The addition-measurability argument in [F9] makes $(s,h)\mapsto\mathbf1_{W_n}(s)\mathbf1_{W_n}(s+h)$ product-measurable, so Tonelli [F5] gives measurability of its section integral $q_n$. Also $0\le q_n(h)\le1$. For fixed $h$, translation invariance [F7] gives $|W_n\setminus(W_n-h)|=|(W_n+h)\setminus W_n|.$ The latter is bounded by $|(W_n+\{0,h\})\setminus W_n|$, so the Van Hove condition [A1] implies $q_n(h)\to1$.

The product-measurable integrand $C(h)\mathbf1_{W_n}(s)\mathbf1_{W_n}(s+h)$ is absolutely integrable: Tonelli and [F9] give
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{W_n}|C(h)|\mathbf1_{W_n}(s+h)\,ds\,dh\le |W_n|\|C\|_1<\infty.$$
In the inner integral of step 1.3 set $h=t-s$; translation invariance [F7]
gives $\int_{W_n}C(t-s)\,dt=\int_{\mathbb R^d}C(h)\mathbf1_{W_n}(s+h)\,dh$.
Fubini [F6] then yields
$$\mathbb E\bigl[(\bar X_{W_n}-\mu)^2\bigr] =\frac1{|W_n|^2}\int_{\mathbb R^d}C(h)|W_n\cap(W_n-h)|\,dh.$$
The overlap factor is the measure of those $s\in W_n$ for which $s+h\in W_n$.

Multiplying the formula in step 2.1 by $|W_n|$ gives $|W_n|\,\mathbb E[(\bar X_{W_n}-\mu)^2]=\int_{\mathbb R^d}C(h)q_n(h)\,dh.$ By [F10], the right side converges to $\int C(h)\,dh$ because $|C(h)q_n(h)|\le|C(h)|\in L^1$. It is therefore bounded; since $|W_n|\to\infty$, step 2.1 implies $\mathbb E[(\bar X_{W_n}-\mu)^2]\to0$.
The mean identity in step 1.2 and the second-moment limit in step 3.1 are exactly $L^2$ convergence to $\mu$ by [F8].

$(e^{i\lambda_1},\ldots,e^{i\lambda_d})$; coordinates and integration are
periodic modulo $2\pi$ in each coordinate. For $n\ge1$, set
$$\Lambda_n:=\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}^d,\qquad N_n:=n^d,$$
and let the $n^d$ Fourier-grid frequencies be
$$\lambda_{n,q}:=2\pi q/n\pmod{2\pi},\qquad q\in\Lambda_n.$$
The known-mean **regular-grid periodogram** is
$$I_n(\lambda):=\frac1{(2\pi)^dN_n} \left|\sum_{j\in\Lambda_n}(Y_j-\mu)e^{-i j\cdot\lambda}\right|^2, \qquad \lambda\in\mathbb T^d.$$
Integration over $\mathbb T^d$ uses product angular Lebesgue measure on the
fundamental cube $[-\pi,\pi)^d$
([[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]]).

For smoothing, let $K:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous, even,
compactly supported, and satisfy $K(0)>0$. For $b>0$, periodize the rescaled
kernel by
$$K_b^{\mathrm{per}}(x):=\sum_{m\in\mathbb Z^d}b^{-d}K((x+2\pi m)/b).$$
Because $K$ has compact support, only finitely many summands are nonzero for
each fixed $x$, so this periodization is well-defined.
For $\lambda\in\mathbb T^d$, when the denominator is positive, set
$$w_{n,q,b}(\lambda):= \frac{K_b^{\mathrm{per}}(\lambda-\lambda_{n,q})} {\sum_{r\in\Lambda_n}K_b^{\mathrm{per}}(\lambda-\lambda_{n,r})}, \qquad \widetilde f_{n,b}(\lambda):= \sum_{q\in\Lambda_n}w_{n,q,b}(\lambda)I_n(\lambda_{n,q}).$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $(Y_j)_{j\in\mathbb Z^d}$ be real square-integrable
random variables with constant mean $\mu$ and lag-dependent covariance
$$c(h):=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{j+h},Y_j),$$
independent of $j$. Assume the Axiom of Choice and Dependent Choice. Then there
is a unique finite positive Radon measure $F$ on the angular torus $\mathbb T^d$
such that
$$c(h)=\int_{\mathbb T^d}e^{ih\cdot\theta}\,F(d\theta), \qquad h\in\mathbb Z^d.$$
For the periodogram $I_n$ of
[[def-regular-grid-periodogram-and-smoother]], define the product Fejer kernel
$$\Phi_n(x):=\frac1{(2\pi)^dn^d} \left|\sum_{j\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}^d}e^{-ij\cdot x}\right|^2 =\prod_{r=1}^d\frac1{2\pi n} \left|\sum_{a=0}^{n-1}e^{-iax_r}\right|^2.$$
Then, for every $n\ge1$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb T^d$,
$$\mathbb E[I_n(\lambda)] =\int_{\mathbb T^d}\Phi_n(\lambda-\theta)\,F(d\theta).$$
The kernel is nonnegative and has integral one with respect to product angular
Lebesgue measure. The spectral measure and density here belong to the
lattice-indexed observations on the dual torus.

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.
$\sin\pi=0$, and $\sin x>0$ for every $x$ with $0<x<\pi$. Thus $\pi$ is the first positive zero of sine.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

The two displayed integrals are well-defined by
[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Fix an integer $d\ge1$ and assume the Axiom of Countable Choice
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). By
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]], every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^d$
is Lebesgue measurable under this assumption; by
[[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], $|\cdot|$ is the resulting
complete Lebesgue measure. A **Van Hove sequence of spatial windows** is a
sequence $(W_n)_{n\ge1}$ of bounded Borel sets
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) in $\mathbb R^d$ with
$0<|W_n|<\infty$ for every $n$, $|W_n|\to\infty$, and
$$\frac{|(W_n+K)\setminus W_n|}{|W_n|}\longrightarrow0 \quad\text{for every compact }K\subseteq\mathbb R^d.$$
Here $|E|$ is Lebesgue measure when $E$ is Lebesgue measurable, and
$W_n+K:=\{x+y:x\in W_n,\ y\in K\}$. As part of the condition, each boundary
excess $(W_n+K)\setminus W_n$ in the display is required to be Lebesgue
measurable. Thus the window volume diverges while every fixed compact spatial
enlargement adds a negligible relative volume.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

Minkowski addition gives $W_n+K=[-1,n+1]\times[-1,2]$. The two closed
rectangles are nested, have finite volume by [F1], and Lebesgue measure is a

$$\frac{|(W_n+K)\setminus W_n|}{|W_n|}

This limit is not zero, contradicting [F1] for the compact $K$; hence the
sequence is not Van Hove.

Let $T\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $d\ge1$, have its relative Borel sigma-algebra, and
let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be one probability space. A **real random
field** indexed by $T$ is a family $X=(X(s))_{s\in T}$ of real random variables
$X(s):\Omega\to\mathbb R$ on that space. This is coordinate measurability:
each map $(s,\omega)\mapsto X(s,\omega)$ with $s$ fixed is measurable in
$\omega$. The field is **jointly measurable** when the map
$(s,\omega)\mapsto X(s,\omega)$ from
$(T\times\Omega,\mathcal B(T)\otimes\mathcal F)$ to
$(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ is measurable. Joint measurability is an
additional hypothesis when a spatial Lebesgue integral is used; it is not part
of coordinate measurability.

Write $\mathcal L(X(s_1),\ldots,X(s_n))$ for the pushforward law of a finite
coordinate tuple ([[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]],
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). The field is **strictly stationary** on $T$ when, for every
finite tuple $s_1,\ldots,s_n\in T$ and every $u\in\mathbb R^d$ for which
$s_i+u\in T$ for all $i$, these joint laws are invariant under the common
translation $s_i\mapsto s_i+u$. This extends the integer-shift convention for
time series in [[def-strict-and-weak-stationarity-for-time-series]] to spatial
indices.

Write $T-T:=\{t-s:s,t\in T\}$ for the set of displacements realized by pairs
of sites.

The field is **wide stationary** when every $X(s)$ is square-integrable, its
mean is one constant $m$, and there is a function $C:T-T\to\mathbb R$ such
that
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X(s),X(t))=C(t-s)\qquad(s,t\in T).$$
For a wide-stationary field on all of $\mathbb R^d$, it is **wide isotropic**
when $C(h)$ depends only on the Euclidean norm $\|h\|$.

For $h\in T-T$ and any $s$ with $s,s+h\in T$, put
$\Delta_hX(s):=X(s+h)-X(s)$. The field is **intrinsically stationary of order
two** when for each $h\in T-T$ the first and second raw moments of
$\Delta_hX(s)$ are finite and independent of the admissible starting site
$s$. Here these moments are $\mathbb E[\Delta_hX(s)]$ and
$\mathbb E[(\Delta_hX(s))^2]$. The common second moment defines the
**variogram**
$$\gamma(h):=\frac12\mathbb E[(\Delta_hX(s))^2].$$
The mean increment may depend on $h$ and need not be zero; no finite second
moment of the field levels themselves is required by this definition.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by

most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be

In ZF,

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

$\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]).
Then $\mathbb T$ is a compact metrizable topological abelian group
([[def-topological-group]]), $\varepsilon$ is an isomorphism of topological
groups, and
$$|zw-z|=|w-1|,\qquad |z^{-1}-w^{-1}|=|z-w|$$
for all $z,w\in\mathbb T$.

$(X_k)_{k < n}$ of compact topological spaces ([[def-compact-space]],
[[def-topological-space]]), the product

$$\prod_{k < n} X_k$$

with the product topology ([[def-product-topology]]) is compact. In particular a

$$c(h):=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{j+h},Y_j),$$

The relation $(a,b) \sim (c,d) \iff a + d = b + c$ on
$\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-integers]]) is an equivalence relation.

quotient set and let $\pi := \{\,(a,C) \in A \times (A/{\sim}) : C = [a]\,\}$,

- (i) there is a function $g : A/{\sim} \to B$ with $g \circ \pi = f$ if and only if $f(a) = f(a')$ whenever $a \sim a'$;

$\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the
plane of pairs of naturals is countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

recursion on $m$ ([[thm-recursion]]) by $2^0 = 1$ and $2^{\sigma(m)} = 2^m + 2^m$,

$$J(m,n) = 2^m \cdot \sigma(n + n), \qquad \text{that is} \qquad J(m,n) = 2^m(2n+1).$$

existence and uniqueness both.

and only if there is a surjection $s : \mathbb{N} \to A$

$$j(a) := \min\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : s(k) = a \,\}.$$

nonempty set countable it suffices to list its elements, repetitions and all.

If $C$ is at most countable and $m\in\mathbb N$, then the finite product $C^m=\prod_{i<m}C$ is at most countable.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]). Its
**nonnegative Lebesgue integral** is
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\left\{\int s\,d\mu:\ s \text{ is nonnegative simple and } 0\le s\le f\right\},$$
where the simple integral on the right is the one from
[[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]].

The set of admissible simple minorants is nonempty because it contains the zero
function, which is simple ([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]).

This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.
